To exult means to feel or show an intense, overflowing joy — especially because of a personal success, victory, or achievement. It's not quiet, private happiness. It's the kind of joy that bursts out of you, that you can't hold back, that makes you want to throw your arms in the air or shout out loud.

Think of a footballer who scores the winning goal in the final second of a match. The way they sprint across the field, screaming with their fists pumping in the air — that is exulting.
What Makes It Different From Just "Being Happy"?

This is the most important thing to understand: exult is not ordinary happiness.

There are many words for positive feelings — happy, glad, pleased, cheerful. These describe everyday good feelings. Exult is on a completely different level. It describes a peak moment of joy — one that is almost too big to contain. The feeling is so intense it spills outward into your body language, your voice, your entire being.

Also — and this is key — exult almost always carries a sense of triumph. The joy usually comes because you succeeded at something, overcame something, or won something. It's not random cheerfulness. It's the specific joy of achievement or victory.
The Two Ways It Is Used

1. Exult in something
This means to feel deep, triumphant joy about your own success or good fortune. The focus is on what you have achieved or gained.

  • She exulted in her victory after years of failure.
  • He exulted in the fact that he had finally finished his novel.
  • The hikers exulted in reaching the summit after the grueling climb.

2. Exult over someone
This means to rejoice at another person's defeat or misfortune. Here, the word takes on a slightly negative shade — it's close to gloating, where your joy comes partly from someone else's loss.

  • The rival team exulted over their opponents' crushing defeat.
  • It's not gracious to exult over someone who has failed.

So remember: exult in = joy about your own success (positive). Exult over = joy at someone else's loss (carries a slightly negative or unsportsmanlike tone).

If you ever need to judge whether "exult" fits a situation, ask yourself two questions:

  • Is this joy extreme — almost bursting at the seams?
  • Does it come from a victory, achievement, or triumph?

If the answer to both is yes, "exult" is the right word. If someone is just mildly pleased or quietly content, "exult" would be too strong.

Since you're a learner, knowing the family of a word is very helpful. Here are the forms of "exult" you'll encounter:

Exultant (adjective) — describes a person or thing that is filled with exultation.

  • The exultant crowd poured into the streets to celebrate.
  • She gave an exultant cry when her name was announced.

Exultation (noun) — the feeling or act of exulting itself.

  • There was pure exultation in his voice when he called to share the news.
  • The winner raised the trophy in exultation.

Exultantly (adverb) — in an exultant manner.

  • "We did it!" she cried exultantly.

Reading a word in many different contexts is one of the best ways to truly absorb it:

  • The prisoners exulted when the gates finally opened and they walked free.
  • The young scientist exulted in the discovery that could change medicine forever.
  • Thousands of fans exulted as the last wicket fell and their team won the series.
  • Try not to exult over your opponent's mistakes — win with grace.
  • He had worked toward this moment for a decade, and now he exulted.

If you ever want to recall this word instantly: to exult is to feel a powerful, often triumphant joy that is so intense it shows on the outside — the kind you feel after a great victory or achievement.
